index.title: How Many Directions the Residuals Fill
index.prompt: You fit a model with 4 parameters to 10 data points by least squares. The fourth feature turns out to be the sum of the first two (a total recorded next to its parts), so in the 10 by 4 matrix A column 4 is column 1 plus column 2. You compute the matrix P that projects onto the column space of A and find tr(P) = 3. For a data vector b the residual is r = b − Pb = (I − P)b. As b ranges over every vector in R^10, the residuals fill a subspace. What is its dimension?
index.answer: 7. Column 4 adds nothing new, so the column space is spanned by columns 1, 2 and 3 and has dimension 3. Every residual is perpendicular to it, and every vector perpendicular to it is its own residual, since its projection is 0. So the residuals fill exactly the directions perpendicular to a 3-dimensional subspace of R^10, a space of dimension 10 - 3 = 7. Dropping column 4 changes neither the column space nor P, so P is also the lesson's formula for the first three columns, with trace 3, and tr(I - P) = 10 - 3 agrees.

prompt.p: Suppose an image search service stores $N$ image feature vectors as the rows of $X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 64}$, and it needs the matrix $S \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$ of pairwise cosine similarities between those vectors.

Explain why it is better to first rescale every row to unit length, forming $W$, and then compute $S = W W^\top$, rather than forming $X X^\top$ and dividing afterwards. Cover both the arithmetic cost and what the diagonal entries of $S$ should equal.

answer.p: Cost. Rescaling is $O(Nd)$ work done once: each of the $N$ rows is multiplied by a single scalar. The alternative first builds $G = X X^\top$ and then divides entry $(i, j)$ by $\lVert x^{(i)} \rVert \lVert x^{(j)} \rVert$, which adds $O(N^2)$ divisions on top of the matrix product, and $N^2$ dwarfs $Nd$ once the image collection grows. That route spends $N^2$ extra operations undoing a scaling that $N$ multiplications would have prevented.
The diagonal. After rescaling, $S_{ij} = \hat{v}^{(i)\top} \hat{v}^{(j)}$ is precisely the cosine similarity, so $S$ is already the matrix that was asked for, and its diagonal is

A diagonal of all ones is a free test: any entry that is not $1$ means that row was never rescaled, most often because the row was all zeros and the rescaling tried to divide $0$ by $0$. With the unscaled $G$, the diagonal holds $\lVert x^{(i)} \rVert_2^2$, which differs from image to image and carries no similarity information at all. Bright or high-contrast pictures happen to produce longer feature vectors, so raw inner products would rank them as similar to everything in the collection.

Write code to compute the row-normalized matrix

answer.p: Three details carry the whole line. $\texttt{(X ** 2).sum(axis=1)}$ sums along each row, giving the $N$ squared norms without a loop. $\texttt{keepdims=True}$ keeps the result shaped $(N, 1)$ instead of $(N,)$, so broadcasting aligns it against the rows of $X$. Drop it and NumPy would try to broadcast a length-$N$ vector across the $d$ columns, which either errors or silently divides the wrong axis when $N = d$. And $\texttt{np.sqrt}$ replaces the banned $\texttt{np.linalg.norm}$.
For the given $X$, row 0 has norm $\sqrt{11}$, row 1 has norm $\sqrt{21}$, and row 2 has norm $3$, so $W$ has rows $(3, -1, 1)/\sqrt{11}$, $(2, 4, 1)/\sqrt{21}$, and $(1/3, 2/3, 2/3)$.

Multiply $X$ by $V$ first, giving $64 \times 8$, then by $U^\top$, which is $8 \times 512$. The cost is the same $524{,}288$ multiplications. Writing $(XU)V^\top$ here would be a different matrix, $XW$, which is only equal when $W$ is symmetric.

prompt.p: A $2 \times 2$ matrix $W$ sends the unit square to a parallelogram of area 3 without flipping the plane over, so $\det W = 3$. A second map first undoes $W$ and then doubles every vector. Its matrix is $2W^{-1}$. What is $\det(2W^{-1})$?

choices.explain: Undoing W divides every area by 3, since det(W^{-1}) det(W) = det(I) = 1. Doubling every vector is the matrix 2I, which doubles both sides of the unit square, so it multiplies areas by 2 · 2 = 4. The product rule gives det(2I) det(W^{-1}) = 4 · 1/3 = 4/3.
This scales the determinant by 2, as if doubling a vector doubled areas. Doubling every vector stretches both directions of the plane, so it multiplies areas by 4: det(2I) = 2 · 2 - 0 · 0 = 4.
This takes det(W^{-1}) to be det W. Undoing a map that triples areas must divide them by 3, since det(W^{-1}) det(W) = det(I) = 1. So the answer is 4 · 1/3, not 4 · 3.

This inverts the 2 as well, as if 2W^{-1} were (2W)^{-1}. The second map doubles after undoing W, so det(2W^{-1}) = det(2I) det(W^{-1}) = 4/3. The value 1/12 belongs to (2W)^{-1}, which halves every vector after undoing W.

theory.title: Which Right-Hand Sides Can Be Reached

prompt.p: For which value of $c$ does $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ have a solution?

answer.p: Look at the rows: row 3 of $A$ is row 1 plus row 2. Entry $i$ of $A\mathbf{x}$ is row $i$ dotted with $\mathbf{x}$, so every output satisfies
A reachable $\mathbf{b}$ must too: $c = 1 + 0 = 1$. For any other $c$ the point $\mathbf{b}$ lies off the column space and there is no solution.

The columns say the same thing. Column 2 is twice column 1, and columns 1 and 3, $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(1, 3, 4)$, are not multiples of each other, so the rank is 2 and the column space is a plane in 3D. The condition $y_3 = y_1 + y_2$ is the equation of that plane, and $c = 1$ is the one value that puts $\mathbf{b}$ on it. Here a solution is $(3, 0, -2)$: row 1 gives $3 + 0 - 2 = 1$, row 2 gives $6 + 0 - 6 = 0$ and row 3 gives $9 + 0 - 8 = 1$.

prompt.p: With that $c$, how many solutions are there? Describe all of them.

answer.p: Rank-nullity for the 3 columns gives $\dim \mathcal{N}(A) = 3 - 2 = 1$. Column 2 minus twice column 1 is $\mathbf{0}$, so $A(-2, 1, 0) = \mathbf{0}$, and that vector spans the null space.
Adding a null vector to a solution gives another solution, so there are infinitely many:
a line in 3D. Every solution has $x_3 = -2$: the first two unknowns only enter through $x_1 + 2x_2$, which must equal 3.

overview: A $3 \times 3$ matrix is built as a sum of three outer products,

prompt.p: What is the rank of $M$?

answer.p: Three terms only say the rank is at most 3. Look for dependencies: $\mathbf{u}_3 = \mathbf{u}_1 + \mathbf{u}_2$, so the third term splits into two outer products, one with $\mathbf{u}_1$ and one with $\mathbf{u}_2$, both with $\mathbf{v}_3$ on the right. Grouping by $\mathbf{u}$,
That is at most rank 2. But $(2, -2, 4)$ is twice $(1, -1, 2)$, so the two terms share a row vector:
$M$ is one outer product of nonzero vectors, so its rank is 1.
Multiplying everything out works too and gives the same answer:
where every row is a multiple of $(1, -1, 2)$.

prompt.p: Change only $\mathbf{v}_3$ so that the rank of $M$ becomes 2, and say why one change cannot make it 3.

answer.p: The rank is 2 when $\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_3$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3$ are independent, because $\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\mathbf{u}_2$ are already independent. With $\mathbf{v}_3 = (0, 0, 0)$ these are $(0, -3, 2)$ and $(1, -4, 4)$, which are not multiples of each other, so the rank is 2. Most other choices work as well.

No choice of $\mathbf{v}_3$ reaches rank 3. Whatever the $\mathbf{v}$'s are, $\mathbf{u}_3 = \mathbf{u}_1 + \mathbf{u}_2$ lets you rewrite $M$ with only $\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\mathbf{u}_2$ on the left, so every column of $M$ is a combination of those two vectors. The rank of a sum of outer products is at most the number of independent $\mathbf{u}$'s (and of independent $\mathbf{v}$'s), not the number of terms.

prompt.p: What is the fitted value of $b$?

answer.p: The model is a curve in $t$ but a straight combination of the unknowns $a$ and $b$, so least squares applies as it does for a line. Row $i$ of $A$ holds what multiplies $a$ and $b$ for reading $i$: a 1 and $t_i^2$.
with the readings in $\mathbf{y} = (2, 1, 3, 7)$.

The normal equations $A^\top A\,\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^\top \mathbf{y}$ use dot products of the columns: $(1,1,1,1) \cdot (1,1,1,1) = 4$, $(1,1,1,1) \cdot (1,0,1,4) = 6$, $(1,0,1,4) \cdot (1,0,1,4) = 18$, and on the right $13$ and $2 + 0 + 3 + 28 = 33$:
Three times the first equation is $12a + 18b = 39$. Subtracting the second gives $6a = 6$, so $a = 1$ and $b = (13 - 4)/6 = 1.5$.
A common slip is to put $t$ in the second column instead of $t^2$. That fits a line, $y = c + m\,t$, a different model.

prompt.p: What is the smallest possible sum of squared errors, the value of $\lVert \mathbf{y} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}} \rVert^2$ at the fit? The model has to give the same value at $t = -1$ and $t = 1$, while the readings there differ. Show that no choice of $a$ and $b$ can do better, whatever happens at the other two readings.

answer.p: Every vector the model can produce, $A\mathbf{x} = (a + b,\ a,\ a + b,\ a + 4b)$, has equal first and third entries. Call that shared value $p$. The squared errors at $t = -1$ and $t = 1$ add up to
by expanding both sides ($2p^2 - 10p + 13$ each). This is at least 0.5 for every $p$, and the other two squared errors are at least 0, so no $(a, b)$ has a total below 0.5.

The fit reaches 0.5. With $a = 1$ and $b = 1.5$ the fitted values are $(2.5, 1, 2.5, 7)$: $p = 2.5$ makes the first part exactly 0.5, and the readings at $t = 0$ and $t = 2$ are matched exactly. The residual is $(-0.5, 0, 0.5, 0)$, and $0.25 + 0 + 0.25 + 0 = 0.5$.

The bound also shows the general rule: readings that the model must fit with one shared value cost at least their spread around their mean, whatever the other parameters do.

theory.title: How Many Directions the Residuals Fill

prompt.p: You fit a model with 4 parameters to 10 data points by least squares. The fourth feature turns out to be the sum of the first two (a total recorded next to its parts), so in the $10 \times 4$ matrix $A$ column 4 is column 1 plus column 2. You compute the matrix $P$ that projects onto the column space of $A$ and find $\operatorname{tr}(P) = 3$. For a data vector $\mathbf{b}$ the residual is $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{b} - P\mathbf{b} = (I - P)\mathbf{b}$.
As $\mathbf{b}$ ranges over every vector in $\mathbb{R}^{10}$, the residuals fill a subspace. What is its dimension?

choices.explain: This reads P^2 = P as P = I, dividing both sides by P. That step needs P to have an inverse, and a projection onto a smaller subspace has none: it sends every vector perpendicular to that subspace to 0. Most b are not in the column space, so most residuals are not zero.

That is the rank of A, the dimension of the column space where the fitted values Pb live. The residual is the part of b that the column space misses, which points in the directions perpendicular to it.
This subtracts the 4 columns, as if each one added a direction. Column 4 is column 1 plus column 2, so the columns span only 3 dimensions, and the residuals keep the other 10 - 3.

Column 4 adds nothing new, so the column space is spanned by columns 1, 2 and 3 and has dimension 3. Every residual is perpendicular to it, and every vector perpendicular to it is its own residual, since its projection is 0. So the residuals fill exactly the directions perpendicular to a 3-dimensional subspace of R^10, a space of dimension 10 - 3 = 7. Dropping column 4 changes neither the column space nor P, so P is also the lesson's formula for the first three columns, with trace 3, and tr(I - P) = 10 - 3 agrees.
b can be any vector in R^10, but the residual cannot. It is always perpendicular to every column of A, which rules out the 3 directions of the column space.

answer.p: Column 4 adds nothing new, so the column space is spanned by columns 1, 2 and 3 and has dimension 3. Every residual is perpendicular to it, and every vector perpendicular to it is its own residual, since its projection is 0. So the residuals fill exactly the directions perpendicular to a 3-dimensional subspace of R^10, a space of dimension 10 - 3 = 7. Dropping column 4 changes neither the column space nor P, so P is also the lesson's formula for the first three columns, with trace 3, and tr(I - P) = 10 - 3 agrees.

theory.title: Removing Two Directions One at a Time
overview: A team wants an embedding $\mathbf{x}$ to carry nothing along two unwanted directions, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$: the cleaned vector should be perpendicular to both. Their code removes the directions one at a time,

prompt.p: What is $\mathbf{x}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1$?

answer.p: First step: the dot product $\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x}$ is 4 and $\lVert \mathbf{v}_1 \rVert^2 = 2$, which gives $\mathbf{x}_1 = (1, 3, 5) - 2(1, 1, 0) = (-1, 1, 5)$, which is perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}_1$.
Second step: the dot product $\mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{x}_1$ is 6 and $\lVert \mathbf{v}_2 \rVert^2 = 2$, which gives $\mathbf{x}_2 = (-1, 1, 5) - 3(0, 1, 1) = (-1, -2, 2)$.

Then $\mathbf{x}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 = -1 - 2 + 0 = -3$. The second step subtracted $3\mathbf{v}_2$, and $\mathbf{v}_2$ has a part along $\mathbf{v}_1$ ($\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 = 1 \ne 0$), so it put back some of the direction the first step had removed. The code's output is perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}_2$ only.

answer.p: This is least squares with the columns $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$: find $\hat{\mathbf{c}}$ with $A^\top A\,\hat{\mathbf{c}} = A^\top \mathbf{x}$, where $A = [\mathbf{v}_1\ \mathbf{v}_2]$.
So $2c_1 + c_2 = 4$ and $c_1 + 2c_2 = 8$, which give $c_1 = 0$ and $c_2 = 4$. The projection is $4\mathbf{v}_2 = (0, 4, 4)$ and the residual is
with length $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$. Check: $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 = 0$.

The code's answer $(-1, -2, 2)$ has length 3, longer than $\sqrt3$. The true residual is the shortest vector $\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}$ over all $\mathbf{p}$ in the plane, so any other leftover, including the code's, is longer.

prompt.p: Change the code's second step so that removing the directions one at a time gives the right answer, and show it does on this example.

answer.p: Sequential removal works when the directions are perpendicular. So first replace $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its residual after projecting onto $\mathbf{v}_1$, which is one step of Gram-Schmidt:

$\mathbf{w}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}_1$ and spans the same plane together with it. Remove $\mathbf{w}$ from $\mathbf{x}_1$ instead of $\mathbf{v}_2$. With the multiple $2\mathbf{w} = (-1, 1, 2)$, which gives the same projection, $(-1, 1, 2) \cdot \mathbf{x}_1 = 1 + 1 + 10 = 12$ and $(-1, 1, 2) \cdot (-1, 1, 2) = 6$, so

theory.title: A Tiny Residual and a Large Error
overview: A solver is asked for $\mathbf{x}$ with $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, where

setup.p: and it returns $\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (2, 0)$. A common test of an answer is its residual $\mathbf{b} - A\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$: if that is small, the answer is accepted.

prompt.p: What is the length of the residual $\mathbf{b} - A\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$?

answer.p: $A\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (2 + 0,\ 2 + 0) = (2, 2)$, so the residual is $(0, 0.01)$, of length 0.01. Measured against $\lVert \mathbf{b} \rVert \approx 2.84$, that is about 0.35%, small enough to pass most tests.

prompt.p: Find the exact solution. How far is $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ from it?

answer.p: The error is $\tilde{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{x} = (1, -1)$, of length $\sqrt2 \approx 1.414$. Relative to $\lVert \mathbf{x} \rVert = \sqrt2$ the answer is off by 100%, with a residual of 0.35%.

prompt.p: Explain the gap between the two numbers using the columns of $A$, and say what it means for checking an answer by its residual.

answer.p: The columns $(1, 1)$ and $(1, 1.01)$ point almost the same way. The parallelogram they span has area $\det A = 0.01$, so $A$ squashes the plane nearly onto a line. A step along $(1, -1)$ takes column 1 minus column 2, so it barely moves the output: $A(1, -1) = (1, 1) - (1, 1.01) = (0, -0.01)$. That is exactly the step from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$.

In general the error and the residual are linked by the inverse: $\mathbf{x} - \tilde{\mathbf{x}} = A^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - A\tilde{\mathbf{x}})$. Here $A^{-1}$ has entries near 100, so it multiplies the residual $(0, 0.01)$ up to $(-1, 1)$. A small residual means a small error only when $A^{-1}$ is not large, that is, when $A$ is well conditioned. The same amplification hits the data: if the second entry of $\mathbf{b}$ had been measured as $2.00$ instead of $2.01$, the exact solution would jump from $(1, 1)$ to $(2, 0)$.

theory.title: Matrices as Linear Maps, Rank, and Outer-Product Decomposition
overview: Recover a matrix from the linear map it performs, find its rank and null space, and split it into the fewest possible rank-one pieces.

setup.p: A robot wrist controller reads four joint angles $x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3$ and outputs three motor commands. For any angle vector

setup.tex: x = \begin{bmatrix} x_0 \\ x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \text{the controller computes} \qquad Ax = \begin{bmatrix} x_0 + x_2 \\ x_1 - x_3 \\ 2x_0 + x_3 \end{bmatrix}.

setup.p: The first command tilts the hand by the sum of two angles, the second turns it by the difference of two others, and the third is a weighted grip drive.

prompt.p: Write down the $3 \times 4$ matrix $A$ that represents this controller.

answer.p: Entry $(i, j)$ of $A$ is the coefficient of $x_j$ in output coordinate $i$. Each output names its inputs directly, so the rows can be transcribed one at a time:

The fastest check is column by column: column $j$ is $Ae_j$. Feeding in $e_0 = (1,0,0,0)^\top$ returns $(1, 0, 2)^\top$, and the first column is indeed $(1, 0, 2)^\top$. The same agreement holds for the other three basis vectors. On a larger map this column test is far quicker than re-reading every row.

prompt.p: Compute $\operatorname{rank}(A)$.

answer.p: The three rows are $r_0 = (1,0,1,0)$, $r_1 = (0,1,0,-1)$, and $r_2 = (2,0,0,1)$. Suppose $\alpha_0 r_0 + \alpha_1 r_1 + \alpha_2 r_2 = 0$. Coordinate $1$ appears only in $r_1$, so $\alpha_1 = 0$. Coordinate $2$ appears only in $r_0$, so $\alpha_0 = 0$. Coordinate $3$ then reads $\alpha_2 = 0$.

The rows are linearly independent, so the row rank is $3$, and $\operatorname{rank}(A) = 3$. Since $A$ has only $3$ rows this is the largest possible value: $A$ has full row rank, and the controller can drive the wrist to any commanded $(y_0, y_1, y_2)$.

prompt.p: Determine $\dim \mathcal{N}(A)$, where $\mathcal{N}(A) = \{ x : Ax = 0 \}$ is the null space, and give a basis for it.

answer.p: By the rank-nullity theorem, for $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$,
so $\dim \mathcal{N}(A) = 4 - 3 = 1$.

To find the basis, solve $Ax = 0$ row by row. The third equation gives $x_3 = -2x_0$. The second then gives $x_1 = x_3 = -2x_0$. The first gives $x_2 = -x_0$. Only $x_0$ remains free, so setting $x_0 = 1$,

Check: $A(1, -2, -1, -2)^\top = (1 - 1,\ -2 + 2,\ 2 - 2)^\top = (0,0,0)^\top$. Physically, that angle configuration leaves every motor idle, so the controller loses one degree of freedom and cannot be inverted.

prompt.p: Any matrix can be rebuilt as a sum of outer products,
with column vectors $u^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and $v^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^4$. For the controller matrix above, find

answer.p: Each term $u^{(i)} v^{(i)\top}$ is an outer product, hence a matrix of rank at most $1$. Rank is subadditive, so $\operatorname{rank}(A) \le I$, and by Part 2 we need $I \ge 3$.

$I = 3$ is achievable: take $u^{(i)} = e_i$, the $i$-th standard basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^3$, and $v^{(i)\top}$ the $i$-th row of $A$. Then $e_i v^{(i)\top}$ is the matrix that is zero everywhere except row $i$, and summing the three rebuilds $A$.

answer.tex: u^{(0)} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},\ v^{(0)} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}; \quad u^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},\ v^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}; \quad u^{(2)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix},\ v^{(2)} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.

answer.result: $I = 3$, with the $u^{(i)}, v^{(i)}$ above (the decomposition is not unique, and the SVD gives another valid choice with the same $I$).

prompt.p: Prove that for any matrix $A$, the smallest $I$ for which a decomposition $A = \sum_{i=0}^{I-1} u^{(i)} v^{(i)\top}$ exists is exactly $\operatorname{rank}(A)$.

answer.p: Two inequalities.

$I \ge \operatorname{rank}(A)$. Every column of $u v^\top$ is a multiple of $u$, so $\operatorname{rank}(uv^\top) \le 1$. Rank is subadditive, $\operatorname{rank}(M + N) \le \operatorname{rank}(M) + \operatorname{rank}(N)$, because the column space of $M + N$ is contained in the sum of the two column spaces. Applying this $I - 1$ times gives $\operatorname{rank}(A) \le I$.

$I \le \operatorname{rank}(A)$. Let $r = \operatorname{rank}(A)$ and let $u^{(0)}, \dots, u^{(r-1)}$ be a basis of the column space $\mathcal{C}(A)$. Every column $a_j$ of $A$ lies in $\mathcal{C}(A)$, so it has a unique expansion $a_j = \sum_{i} c_{ij} u^{(i)}$. Collecting the coefficients into vectors $v^{(i)}$ with $v^{(i)}_j = c_{ij}$ gives
a decomposition with $I = r$ terms. Both bounds together give minimum $I = \operatorname{rank}(A)$.

prompt.p: Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ have rank $r$. Storing $A$ densely costs $mn$ numbers, and storing the $r$ outer-product factors costs $r(m + n)$ numbers.
Determine exactly when the factored form is cheaper, and evaluate the condition for a $4096 \times 4096$ weight matrix with $r = 8$ (the setting a LoRA adapter targets).

answer.p: The factored form stores $r$ vectors of length $m$ and $r$ of length $n$, so it is cheaper exactly when
For $m = n$ this simplifies to $r < m/2$: a square matrix pays off as soon as its rank is below half its dimension.

For $m = n = 4096$ and $r = 8$: dense storage is $4096^2 = 16{,}777{,}216$ numbers, factored storage is $8 \cdot 8192 = 65{,}536$ numbers, a $256\times$ reduction. The threshold $mn/(m+n) = 2048$ is far above $8$, which is why low-rank adapters are so cheap, and also why they can only express updates that genuinely live in a low-dimensional subspace.

prompt.p: Let $B \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 5}$ with $\operatorname{rank}(B) = 2$, and let $A$ be the matrix from this problem. Which statement about $\operatorname{rank}(AB)$ is correct?

choices: A. $\operatorname{rank}(AB) = 3$, because $A$ has full row rank.
E. There is not enough information to bound $\operatorname{rank}(AB)$.

answer.p: Rank is submultiplicative under products:
The reason is that the columns of $AB$ are $A$ applied to the columns of $B$, so $\mathcal{C}(AB) \subseteq A\,\mathcal{C}(B)$, whose dimension cannot exceed $\dim \mathcal{C}(B) = 2$.

A is wrong because full row rank in $A$ cannot manufacture rank that $B$ does not have. B and D confuse rank with matrix shape: rank never exceeds $\min(m, n)$, and ranks do not add under multiplication. This bound is why stacking two low-rank layers with no nonlinearity between them buys you nothing.

parts.requirement: Do not use np.linalg, do not use the @ operator or .T, and do not use any loop.

prompt.p: Run the following starter code:
Write one line of code that computes the matrix-vector product $Ax$ and names it $\texttt{y}$.

answer.p: Broadcasting does the work. $\texttt{x}$ has shape $(4,)$ and $\texttt{A}$ has shape $(3, 4)$, so NumPy stretches $\texttt{x}$ across the three rows, giving an elementwise product whose entry $(i, j)$ is $A_{ij} x_j$. Summing along $\texttt{axis=1}$ collapses the $j$ index, which is precisely $y_i = \sum_j A_{ij} x_j$.

For the given values, $y = (1 + 3,\ 2 - 4,\ 2 + 4)^\top = (4, -2, 6)^\top$. Note this trick costs $mn$ memory for the intermediate product, so it is a constraint-satisfying answer rather than the way you would write production code. There, $\texttt{A @ x}$ calls BLAS and allocates nothing.
